2024 · CVPR 2024 · Benchmarks & Evals

EvalCrafter: Benchmarking and Evaluating Large Video Generation Models

A 700-prompt benchmark and a battery of 17 objective metrics across four aspects — visual quality, text-video alignment, motion quality, temporal consistency — for text-to-video models, with a linear-regression step that fits those metrics to human ratings (1,024 kept from 8,647 collected) rather than trusting FVD or Inception Score alone.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By late 2023 a wave of text-to-video (T2V) systems — ModelScope, ZeroScope, VideoCrafter, Show-1, Hotshot-XL, and closed commercial services like Runway's Gen2 and PikaLab — had shipped, but the field still evaluated them almost entirely with two borrowed image/GAN metrics: Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) and Inception Score (IS). Both are distribution-matching metrics: FVD needs a reference set of real videos and only checks whether the generated distribution looks statistically similar to it, and IS only checks how diverse and classifiable the generated content is. Neither measures whether the video actually matches its text prompt, whether the motion looks right, or whether it stays temporally consistent from frame to frame.

The paper's framing is that T2V models "are often trained on very large datasets with multi-aspect abilities," so judging them by a single distributional number misses most of what differs between systems. It also notes a growing practical problem: several of the strongest T2V systems (Gen2, PikaLab) are closed commercial services — no weights, no training data, sometimes only watermarked output — so any evaluation protocol has to work from generated video alone, the same constraint LLM evaluation had already been forced to confront with GPT-4-class models. EvalCrafter's gap, in short: no existing T2V benchmark combined (a) a prompt set built to stress specific, checkable attributes, (b) a wide battery of aspect-specific automatic metrics, and (c) an explicit calibration step tying those metrics back to human judgment.

// how it works

The method

EvalCrafter has three parts: a prompt benchmark, a metric battery, and a human-alignment step that fits the metrics to people's actual preferences.

1. Building the 700-prompt benchmark

The authors first mined over 600k real prompts from T2V Discord communities (FullJourney, PikaLab), filtering to roughly 200k after removing duplicates and junk, and used that corpus only to learn the shape of real usage — prompt length (90% fall in the 3–40 word range) and four recurring meta-subject classes: human, animal, object, landscape. From there, prompts were not simply sampled from the wild; they were generated with GPT-4 against structured templates ("Describe a scene about {count|humans}, {motions|None} … return in json format …"), producing a natural-language description paired with structured metadata (gender, race, activity, age, etc. for a human-class prompt). Because GPT-4's generated attributes and its generated description weren't always consistent with each other, the authors added a second GPT-4 pass that asks, for each attribute, "does the description actually support this metadata value — yes or no," filtering out anything that fails. Real-world prompts and existing T2I evaluation prompts (DALL-Eval, DrawBench) were folded in the same way. The final 700-prompt set breaks down as Human 280, Object 210, Animal 140, Landscape 70 (summing to 700), further split into three sub-types — Realistic 450, Style 150, Camera-motion 100 (also summing to 700) — with 50 distinct styles and 20 camera-motion prompt templates in circulation, and an average prompt length of 12.3 words.

2. Seventeen objective metrics across four aspects

Rather than one number, EvalCrafter scores every generated video on 17 metrics grouped into four aspects:

  • Visual quality: VQAA and VQAT (aesthetic and technical scores from Dover, a video-quality model trained on real user rankings) and Inception Score.
  • Text-video alignment: CLIP-Score (frame-wise CLIP similarity between prompt and video), a new SD-Score the paper proposes (embedding similarity between the generated video and five SDXL-generated reference images of the same prompt, N₁=5, meant to catch "concept forgetting" when a T2V model is fine-tuned from a text-to-image backbone), BLIP-BLEU (BLEU between the prompt and BLIP-2's caption of the generated video), and three attribute-grounded scores computed via SAM-Track object detection: Detection-Score (is the named object present), Count-Score (is the count right), Color-Score (is the color right) — plus Celebrity ID Score (DeepFace distance to real celebrity photos, for human-class prompts) and OCR-Score (Word/Character/Normalized-Edit-Distance error rates from PaddleOCR, for prompts asking the model to render text).
  • Motion quality: Action-Score (Kinetics-400 action-classification accuracy via a VideoMAE V2 model on the MMAction2 toolbox) and Flow-Score (average RAFT optical flow magnitude), plus a derived Motion Amplitude Classification Score that checks whether a video crosses a flow threshold (ρ = 5, chosen "based on our subjective observation") consistently with what the prompt asked for.
  • Temporal consistency: Warping Error (pixel-wise difference between a frame and its optical-flow-warped predecessor), CLIP-Temp (cosine similarity between consecutive frames' CLIP embeddings), and Face Consistency (cosine similarity of every frame's face embedding to the first frame's).

3. Calibrating the metrics to human opinion

Five of the eight T2V systems the paper otherwise evaluates — ModelScope, ZeroScope, Gen2, Floor33 Pictures, and PikaLab — were rendered against the benchmark's initial 512-prompt set (later expanded to the released 700), producing roughly 2.5k videos. Seven human raters scored each video, 1–5, on five aspects (Video Quality, Text-and-Video Alignment, Motion Quality, Temporal Consistency, and a fifth "Subjective Likeness" aspect that the paper leaves un-aligned and reports raw). That produced 8,647 raw ratings, filtered down to 1,024 "most objective and professional" scores — the paper does not specify the filtering rule beyond that phrase. A linear regression is then fit per aspect, mapping the aspect's objective metrics onto the human scores by minimizing residual sum of squares, using an 80/20 train/verify split; the fitted weights become the "human-aligned" score reported for every system, including the three (VideoCrafter1, Show-1, Hotshot-XL) that were never part of the human study at all.

SSD = 1M Σi 1N Σt 1N₁ Σk cos( emb(xti), emb(dki) ) // SD-Score: mean CLIP-embedding similarity between every video frame xᵢₜ and N₁=5 SDXL reference images dᵢₖ generated from the same prompt
// what they found

The results

Eight systems went through the full 17-metric battery: ModelScope, ZeroScope, Floor33 Pictures, PikaLab, Gen2, VideoCrafter1, Show-1, and Hotshot-XL. On the final human-aligned scores (which combine the metrics per aspect via the fitted regression), Gen2 tops Visual Quality (62.51) and Motion Quality (56.43), Show-1 tops Text-Video Alignment (62.07), and PikaLab tops Temporal Consistency (65.41) — no single system wins on all four aspects, which the paper reads as evidence that single-dimension evaluation is insufficient (Finding #1).

The paper's central methodological claim is that the fitted alignment step beats naive averaging of the raw metrics. On visual quality it's a modest win (Spearman ρ 55.4 for "Ours" vs. 55.0 for a plain average of VQAA/VQAT/IS; Kendall ϕ 41.1 vs. 41.0). On temporal consistency it's 56.7 vs. 54.4 (ρ) and 41.5 vs. 38.9 (ϕ). On text-video alignment, 32.3 vs. 31.9 (ρ) and 22.5 vs. 22.7 (ϕ, a case where the naive average is very slightly higher on this one statistic). The most dramatic gap is on motion amplitude: every individual metric that feeds it is negatively correlated with human judgment — Action-Score −14.9, Motion AC-Score −22.1, Flow-Score −43.3 (Spearman) — and their plain average lands at −38.2, worse than two of the three but not as bad as Flow-Score's −43.3. The fitted "Ours" score is +45.0. The paper's own explanation (Finding #6) is that users prefer subtle motion, so any metric that rewards more/larger movement points the wrong way; the regression learns to invert that signal rather than simply average it away.

Beyond the headline numbers, the paper reports ten "Findings," several with specific evidence: camera-motion prompts are followed by none of the evaluated models (Finding #4); resolution barely tracks visual quality — Gen2 (896×512) and Hotshot-XL (672×384) have small resolutions but are both competitive in visual quality, while the two actually-smallest resolutions in the lineup (ModelScope 256×256, Show-1 576×320) are the two lowest-ranked systems on Visual Quality (Finding #5); larger flow doesn't mean users like it more, and PikaLab/Gen2 (both low average flow) are the models users rate highest on motion (Finding #6); and CLIP-Score, despite being "a widely used metric in previous works," correlates weakly with human judgment (Spearman 6.3, Kendall 4.3) compared to BLIP-BLEU's 26.7/19.0 in the same text-video-alignment aspect (Finding #9).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

EvalCrafter's central idea — don't trust a single distributional metric, build a battery, and calibrate it against people — is sound and was, at the time, genuinely new for T2V. But several parts of the paper's own reporting undercut confidence in exactly the numbers it wants readers to trust.

The human-aligned leaderboard is partly extrapolated, not validated. Section 4.5 states the user study covers "five state-of-the-art methods of ModelScope, ZeroScope, Gen2, Floor33, and PikaLab" — 2.5k videos, 7 raters, 8,647 raw scores. The regression that turns raw metrics into the "human-aligned" scores in Table 2 is fit on that five-system population. But Table 2 reports human-aligned scores for eight systems — the same five, plus VideoCrafter1, Show-1, and Hotshot-XL, none of which any human ever rated in this study (Table 4, the raw 17-metric matrix, covers the same eight-system population without any fitting). Their "human-aligned" ranks (VideoCrafter1 2nd on Visual Quality, Show-1 1st on Text-Video Alignment) are the fitted coefficients applied out-of-sample, with no held-out human data to confirm the fit generalizes to systems it never saw.

The paper's own count of how many systems fed that regression is internally inconsistent. Immediately after naming the five rated systems, the fitting-procedure sentence says "we randomly choose 80% samples from four different methods as the fitting samples and left the rest 20% samples to verify" — four, not five, with no explanation for which system (or whether one was held out entirely, as opposed to sampled) accounts for the discrepancy. We checked appendix D for a resolution; D.9 addresses a different count question (whether the study used 512 or 700 prompts) but never revisits the four-vs-five methods gap.

No inter-rater agreement statistic is reported anywhere in the paper. Appendix D.2 does describe a rater-qualification gate — each candidate labels 100 pre-labeling tasks and needs above 90% accuracy to be admitted, otherwise “we will consider another supplier” — which is more quality control than the critique above might suggest. But qualification against a known answer key is a different measurement from agreement among raters on the subjective 1–5 scales, and only the former is reported. Seven raters scored 1–5 per aspect, but the paper reports only how well the aggregated/averaged human score correlates with the objective metrics (Table 3/5) — never a Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa, ICC, or similar measure of how much the seven raters agreed with each other. The limitations section admits "the labels used for alignment are collected from only fewer human annotators, which may introduce some bias," without quantifying how much. Filtering 8,647 raw scores down to the 1,024 that were kept is also unexplained beyond "most objective and professional" — no threshold, no worked criterion.

Two of the paper's own correlation tables disagree on a specific cell. The main-text Table 3 reports VQAA's Spearman correlation with human judgment as 42.1; the appendix's "whole results" Table 5 reports 47.8 for the same aspect × metric cell (we re-verified both independently from the PDF's own word positions, so this isn't a misread on our part). The aspect's Avg. row also differs slightly (55.0 vs. 54.9). Every "Ours" value the paper's method produces is identical across both tables — it's specifically the individual-metric row that doesn't reconcile.

The appendix's own callout of "unreliable" metrics undersells its own table. Appendix B.2, discussing Table 5 directly, names "Color-Score and OCR-Score" as text-video-alignment metrics with negative correlation to human judgment. The same table shows four negative metrics in that aspect, not two — SD-Score (−2.8), Color-Score (−5.5), OCR-Score (−8.3), and Celebrity ID Score at −26.0, more than three times as negative as either metric the text actually names, and the second-most-negative of any individual metric in the paper (after Flow-Score's −43.3). A reader relying on that prose alone would come away thinking Celebrity ID Score is a reliable alignment signal; the table beside it says the opposite.

baselines

Eight systems, reasonably representative of the Oct 2023 T2V landscape (open-source: ModelScope, ZeroScope, VideoCrafter1, Show-1, Hotshot-XL; commercial/closed: Gen2, PikaLab, Floor33/Morph Studio). All were current at time of writing; the paper explicitly frames the benchmark as a snapshot meant for "periodic updates" (Appendix D.3), not a permanent leaderboard.

contamination

Not the LLM-style training-data-leakage risk — the concern here is methodological rather than data leakage: three of the eight leaderboard entries (VideoCrafter1, Show-1, Hotshot-XL) never had a human rate them, so their "human-aligned" scores are the regression extrapolated outside the population it was fit on.

what's missed

No inter-rater agreement statistic for the 7-person panel; no disclosed rule for the 8,647→1,024 rating filter; no error analysis of the pipeline metrics that depend on other models' accuracy (SAM-Track for Detection/Count/Color-Score, DeepFace for Celebrity ID Score, PaddleOCR for OCR-Score) under video-generation artifacts specifically.

would raise confidence

Human ratings for all eight evaluated systems (not five of eight); a stated, reproducible filter for which of the 8,647 raw scores were kept; an explicit reconciliation of the four-vs-five-methods regression-population sentence; and a single, consistent correlation table (the main text and appendix currently print two different Spearman values for VQA_A).

// bottom line

The paper's most convincing evidence — that naively averaging motion metrics anti-correlates with what people actually prefer (−38.2 Spearman) while the fitted score flips that to +45.0 — is a genuinely useful empirical result for anyone building a T2V metric. But three of the eight systems on the final leaderboard were scored by a regression that never saw a human rating of them, the paper's own two correlation tables disagree on three of the sixteen rows they share, and the human-study design (rater count, filtering criterion, agreement) is under-documented relative to how much weight the "human-aligned" score is asked to carry.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. EvalCrafter replaces the single FVD/IS number T2V papers had been reporting with a 700-prompt benchmark and 17 metrics across four aspects (visual quality, text-video alignment, motion quality, temporal consistency), then fits a linear regression per aspect to calibrate those metrics against human ratings (1,024 kept from 8,647 collected).
  2. The clearest evidence for why that calibration matters: on motion amplitude, every individual raw metric — and their naive average (−38.2 Spearman) — anti-correlates with human preference, because people prefer subtle motion while the raw metrics reward more of it; the fitted score flips this to +45.0.
  3. Read the appendix before trusting the leaderboard: the human-alignment regression was fit on ratings from only 5 of the 8 evaluated systems (extrapolated to the other 3), the paper's fitting-procedure text says "four different methods" where the study description says "five," and the main-text and appendix correlation tables print two different Spearman values (42.1 vs. 47.8) for the same VQA_A cell.
